editor_spans.body: The speech's diagnosis is about history: Ravenscraig shut and Leigh's pits closed by decisions taken far away, with no plan for what came next. But the remedies on offer are small next to that loss. They are £10 million for defence colleges, matched by Holyrood. They are a £1 billion research pot spread across the whole UK. And they are a promise to 'explore' devolving innovation and employability funding. Moving decisions closer to Motherwell does not by itself rebuild what a closed steelworks took away. The capital, the orders and the industrial base still have to come from somewhere.

The most consequential line may be the one about procurement, and it is not a devolution policy at all. Burnham chose Falkirk-built buses for Manchester over the cheapest bid. He wants all UK public buying to work that way. That would be a central, national lever that reverses the long-standing Whitehall habit of judging contracts on price alone. If it happens, it would shape where things get made far more than any regional funding deal. Watch whether the Treasury's rules actually change.

The offer is also framed as a competition. Scottish towns risk being 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up'. Holyrood's own reform timetable is dismissed as too slow. And UK-level funds are put on the table for Scotland's regions. That continues a trend from the 2020 Internal Market Act, when Westminster took powers to spend directly in devolved areas. A friendlier tone does not change the direction: the UK government is building its own channels to Scottish places. Holyrood is left to join in or be cast as the obstacle.
